title: An address failed and also signed in, in a way that looks like an attack
why: The sign-in was over ODBC/JDBC or on a generic account, or came from a new address trying three or more account names. Attackers sign in with what works, then keep trying other accounts and files.
todo: Confirm today who this address is. If nobody can, follow the incident response steps.

title: Hosted file names are listed without sign-in
why: Attack tools start here. They use the list to pick which files to try.
todo: Turn on Filter Databases and Deny Guest and auto-login, then run the check again.

title: An address failed and also signed in
why: One or two failures followed by a sign-in on a person's own account is usually staff mistyping. Until someone confirms the address, it counts as possible compromise.
todo: Confirm who this address belongs to and mark it as known.

title: An ODBC/JDBC connection reached the server
why: An attacker who gets in first time leaves no failed sign-in. Each address should match a SQL or BI tool someone can name.
todo: Confirm which tool this is. If nobody can, treat it as possible compromise.

title: Failed sign-ins through ODBC/JDBC (port 2399)
why: The attacks spray port 2399 as well as 443, and a web rate limiter or firewall in front of 443 doesn't see it.
todo: Close port 2399 at the firewall, or allow it only from your SQL or BI tools' addresses.

title: Many failed sign-ins in a short time
why: Twenty or more failures in ten minutes across several names is password spraying. On one name it's usually a person or a saved password retrying.
todo: Allow-list ports 443 and 2399 or use a VPN, and check the account names tried.

title: One address tried three or more account names
why: This is the password-spraying pattern. A low count per account is no comfort, because spraying stays under the account lockout.
todo: Use strong unique passwords, and allow-list ports 443 and 2399 or use a VPN.

title: One address tried three or more files
why: Attack tools work through every hosted file they can list.
todo: Use strong unique passwords, and allow-list ports 443 and 2399 or use a VPN.

title: Sign-ins tried on a generic account name
why: Blank, Admin, Guest, web, user, api, test and filemaker are what attack tools try first. From staff it's often a harmless saved blank attempt.
todo: Confirm who this address is, and remove or rename generic accounts.

title: An address failed and never signed in
why: No sign-in appears in the Access logs supplied. On its own this is lower risk, but it's still someone trying to get in.
todo: Check the address against the people you know, then allow-list ports 443 and 2399 or use a VPN.

title: Failures older than the Access log
why: The failures are older than the Access log, so a sign-in can't be ruled out. This is a limit on the verdict, never a pass.
todo: Check any older copies of the Access log, and keep logs for longer from now on.

title: Failed sign-ins from the server itself
why: This is usually a script or schedule with a stale password. It isn't an attack, but it shouldn't be failing.
todo: Find the schedule and fix its password.

title: Failed sign-ins with no other warning sign
why: The address has connected before and none of the warning patterns match.
todo: Nothing unless it keeps happening.

title: A FileMaker Pro build with a published security issue connected
why: The issue is in the client, so updating the server doesn't fix it.
todo: Update FileMaker Pro on the staff computers listed.

title: An Admin Console sign-in from a new address
why: Admin Console access controls the whole server.
todo: Confirm today who signed in.

title: The Admin Console account has a guessable name
why: A name such as admin gives an attacker half the login.
todo: Rename the Admin Console account and use a strong unique password.

title: Failed Admin Console sign-ins
why: A repeating failure from one address usually means a tool still holds an old password. From an unknown address it's an attempt.
todo: Confirm who this address is, and restrict Admin Console access to known addresses.

title: A large volume of records went to one client
why: Files with Guest or auto-login sign in without a single failure, so volume is how a download shows up.
todo: Confirm who this client is and whether the download was expected.

title: Many tables read by a new address or a generic account
why: Reading across many tables in ten minutes is what a bulk download looks like.
todo: Confirm who this client is and whether the access was expected.

title: A burst of Data API, OData or XML record calls
why: The attacks pull records 200 at a time across every layout available.
todo: Confirm which integration this is. If nobody can, treat it as possible compromise.

title: A PHP or XML page answered a request
why: Scanners ask every server for these, so refusals are noise. A page that answered is not.
todo: Check the server for PHP, then patch or remove it, and turn off XML publishing if it's unused.

title: A port that should be closed is open
why: Local-only and remote-access ports shouldn't answer from the internet. Port forwarders can show ports open when nothing is listening, so confirm on the server.
todo: Close it at the firewall, or restrict it to known addresses.

title: An admin sign-in page is open to any address
why: Anyone on the internet can try passwords against it.
todo: Restrict the page to known addresses.

title: PHP answers from the internet
why: An upgrade may have left an old PHP engine behind.
todo: Find its version on the server, then patch or remove it.

title: XML publishing is on
why: An unused service is something else for an attacker to try.
todo: Turn it off if it's unused.

title: The certificate needs attention
why: A self-signed or default certificate lets clients be intercepted.
todo: Install a trusted custom certificate.

title: Port 80 serves content over plain HTTP
why: Port 80 should answer only with a redirect to HTTPS.
todo: Redirect it to HTTPS.

title: The exposure check flagged a path
why: The check marked this path for review.
todo: Compare it with the services this server is meant to offer.

title: An open port with no intended service behind it
why: Every open port is one more way in, and the automated attacks start by finding what answers. A port nobody needs shouldn't be reachable at all.
todo: If nothing needs it, close it at the firewall. If something does, tick that service under Intended services on Server Detail, and restrict the port to the addresses that use it.

title: A web service answers that isn't ticked as intended
why: Once the automated attacks find a way in, they pull records through the Data API and OData. A service nobody uses is a way in nobody watches.
todo: Turn it off in the Admin Console if nothing uses it. If something does, tick it under Intended services on Server Detail.

title: A server setting goes against Claris's security advice
why: The scan reads the server's settings through the Admin API with its own sign-in, and compares them with Claris's Security Guide.
todo: Change the setting in the Admin Console.

title: A server setting to confirm
why: The setting can be right for some solutions and wrong for others, so someone who knows the solution has to say.
todo: Confirm the setting is needed, or change it in the Admin Console.

title: A critical published issue affects this server's version
why: A published issue with a CVSS score of 9 or more. Attackers look for servers that haven't been updated.
todo: Update FileMaker Server to the release that fixes it.

title: A serious published issue affects this server's version
why: A published issue with a CVSS score of 7 to 8.9.
todo: Update FileMaker Server to the release that fixes it.

title: A published issue affects this server's version
why: A published issue, or a security fix Claris lists only in its release notes.
todo: Update FileMaker Server to the release that fixes it.

title: FileMaker Server is behind its latest release
why: No published issue affects this version, but later releases carry fixes, and Claris recommends updating promptly.
todo: Plan the update to the latest release.

title: HTTPS doesn't tell browsers to stay on HTTPS (HSTS)
why: Without HSTS, a browser can be sent to plain HTTP first. Claris turns HSTS on once a custom certificate is installed.
todo: Turn on HSTS: install a trusted custom certificate, or check the web server's settings.

title: HTTPS still accepts TLS 1.0 or 1.1
why: Old TLS versions have known weaknesses, and Claris's guide says to use current TLS only.
todo: Turn off TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on the server's web server.

title: Screen sharing answers with no password
why: Anyone on the internet who connects gets the server's screen, keyboard and mouse, with nothing to guess.
todo: Set a password for screen sharing, or turn it off, and close the port to the internet.

title: A critical published issue affects a service the internet can reach
why: A published issue rated Critical (CVSS 9 or above) in a service that answers from outside. Attack tools try these soon after they're published.
todo: Update the service today, or close its port to the internet until it's updated.

title: A serious published issue affects a service the internet can reach
why: A published issue rated High (CVSS 7 to 8.9) in a service that answers from outside.
todo: Update the service, or allow its port only from known addresses until it's updated.

title: Published issues affect a service the internet can reach
why: Published issues rated Medium or Low in a service that answers from outside. Each is a smaller risk, but they add up.
todo: Include the service in the server's next round of updates.

title: Remote Desktop shows its sign-in screen to anyone
why: Without Network Level Authentication, anyone can reach the Windows sign-in screen without authenticating, and Remote Desktop's worst published issues (BlueKeep) need exactly that.
todo: Turn on Network Level Authentication, and allow Remote Desktop only over a VPN.

title: File sharing only speaks SMB1
why: SMB1 is retired and has no modern protections. The WannaCry and NotPetya worms spread through it.
todo: Turn off SMB1, and close file sharing (445) to the internet.

title: The operating system is out of support
why: A release past its end of support gets no security fixes at all, so every issue found from now on stays open.
todo: Upgrade the server to a supported release of its operating system.

title: The operating system is on extended support only
why: Standard support has ended. Security fixes still come, but only through Ubuntu Pro (ESM) or Debian LTS.
todo: Confirm the server gets extended security updates (for Ubuntu, that Ubuntu Pro is attached), and plan the upgrade.

title: Services give away their versions before sign-in
why: A version tells an attacker which published issues to try. Hiding it doesn't patch anything, but it stops the server standing out in a search.
todo: Hide the version where the software allows it: nginx server_tokens off, Apache ServerTokens Prod, PHP expose_php Off. OpenSSH always sends its version.

title: The server gives away its computer and domain names
why: Remote Desktop and file sharing answer the first step of a sign-in with the computer and domain names. Attackers use them to aim password spraying.
todo: Close Remote Desktop and file sharing to the internet, or allow them only over a VPN.
